name: Fred Atkins
bio: Billiard-marker, bookmaker's clerk and music-hall comedian — 'I am twenty years old' on oath in April 1895 — introduced to Taylor by Schwabe in November 1892 and taken to Paris by Wilde that month as nominal private secretary. He lived and worked blackmail with the bookmaker James Burton; on the stand he denied any impropriety with Wilde, and on recall was proved to have lied on oath about a Rochester Row arrest (a gentleman found naked in bed with him, money demanded) and was ordered from the box. The judge's summing-up called him 'a most reckless, unreliable, unscrupulous, and untruthful witness' (as quoted by the Letters editors), and the jury found Wilde not guilty on every Atkins count.
bio_sources: Atkins's testimony and recall, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 206-210, 216-218.
Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction pp. 72, 74 (perjury; not-guilty verdict).
Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 714 n. 1 (the judge's phrase; Wilde acquitted of the Atkins charges).
bio_note: Age ('I am twenty years old') from Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 206; the judge repeats it in his summing-up ('Atkins is now twenty years of age'). Mary Applegate's stained-sheets testimony (Hyde p. 211) is the only circumstantial support for the Paris allegation. Occupations and the judge's 'most reckless, unreliable, unscrupulous, and untruthful witness' from Complete Letters (2000), p. 714 n. 1. No dates recorded.
